target: La sal está en el armario de la cocina.
english: The salt is in the kitchen cabinet.
tip: La sal – feminine. Nouns ending in consonant don't follow -o/-a rule.

target: Se me hace bola tener que leer todo este informe.
english: I find it overwhelming to have to read this whole report.
tip: 'Se me hace bola' – it 'turns into a ball' in my mouth, like food you can't swallow. Spain's go-to idiom for tasks that feel impossibly heavy, like this 'informe'.

target: Me lleva unos veinte minutos llegar al trabajo en carro.
english: It takes me about twenty minutes to get to work by car.
tip: "llevar" + time = to take (time). Like gustar, the time is the subject: "twenty minutes takes me." Also: "me llevó" (past).

target: Me pongo crema en las manos porque están muy secas.
english: I put cream on my hands because they're very dry.
tip: Están secas, not son secas: the dryness is a fixable current state – exactly estar's job. Son would make 'dry' the hands' permanent personality.

target: Lo cambiaron por otro modelo más nuevo.
english: They exchanged it for another newer model.
tip: Trading? That's por. 'Lo cambiaron por otro modelo' – por marks what you swap or pay in exchange, where English just says 'for.'

target: Quiero tres noches.
english: I want three nights.
tip: Sounds blunt? 'Quiero tres noches' is normal transactional Spanish – 'I want' isn't rude at a hotel desk. Save 'quisiera' for extra-polite requests.

target: Avísame cuando termines.
english: Let me know when you finish.
tip: Why 'termines,' not 'terminas'? 'Cuando' pointing at the future takes subjunctive – the finishing hasn't happened yet, so Spanish flags it as not-yet-real.

target: Hace buen tiempo hoy.
english: The weather is nice today.
tip: "Hacer" is used for weather: "hace calor" (it's hot), "hace frío" (it's cold).

target: No sé dónde está.
english: I don't know where it is.
tip: 'Sé' is knowing facts and info – like 'dónde está.' Knowing a person or place switches to conocer. Two knows in Spanish, and they never swap jobs.

target: Me gusta mucho esta ciudad.
english: I really like this city.
tip: "Gustar" works backwards from English: the thing you like is the subject. "Me gusta la ciudad" = the city pleases me. "Me gustan los gatos" = cats please me (plural).

target: Nos hace ilusión el viaje.
english: We're thrilled about the trip.
tip: Ilusión here isn't 'illusion' – it's excited anticipation. Nos hace ilusión: the trip makes-us-thrill. Classic false friend: no delusions involved.

target: La playa está muy cerca.
english: The beach is very close.
tip: 'Muy' (very) goes before adjectives/adverbs. For nouns, use 'mucho/a': 'mucha hambre,' not 'muy hambre.'

target: Yo duermo solo seis horas.
english: I only sleep six hours.
tip: Trap: 'duermo solo seis horas' could also read 'I sleep ALONE six hours' – 'solo' means both only and alone. Context (or using 'solamente') breaks the tie.

target: Hace frío, ponte un abrigo.
english: It's cold, put on a coat.
tip: Hace frío is literally 'it makes cold' – Spanish uses hacer for weather. The same hace means 'ago' with time (hace dos años), so context picks the meaning.

target: Mi hijo tiene tres años.
english: My son is three years old.
tip: Tener + años = to be X years old (Spanish uses 'have' not 'be').

target: La cerveza es muy barata aquí.
english: Beer is very cheap here.
tip: English drops the article for beer-in-general; Spanish can't: 'la cerveza es muy barata' = beer as a whole is cheap. Generalizations always take el/la/los/las.

target: Ella se fue sin decir adiós.
english: She left without saying goodbye.
tip: English says 'without sayING'; Spanish never puts -ing after a preposition: 'sin decir adiós' = without to-say goodbye. After sin, always the infinitive.

target: Hay cien personas en la sala.
english: There are a hundred people in the room.
tip: 'Hay' = there is / there are. Unlike 'ser/estar', 'hay' is the same for singular and plural. Comes from 'haber'.

target: La casa de mis padres es grande.
english: My parents' house is big.
tip: No apostrophe-s exists in Spanish: you say 'the house of my parents' – 'la casa de mis padres.' Owned thing first, then 'de' + owner, every time.

target: Lo que me dijiste ayer me sorprendió.
english: What you told me yesterday surprised me.
tip: "Lo que" = what / that which: "Lo que dices es verdad." Used for abstract ideas or things not yet identified.

target: Hoy es el primer día de la primavera.
english: Today is the first day of spring.
tip: Why 'primer,' not 'primero'? Before a masculine singular noun, primero (and tercero) drop the -o: 'el primer día.' Everywhere else the -o stays.

target: Date prisa, el autobús sale en cinco minutos!
english: Hurry up, the bus leaves in five minutes!
tip: 'Date prisa' is literally 'give yourself haste' – in Spanish you hand hurry to yourself. Same logic as 'darse cuenta' (give yourself account = realize).

target: Soy alérgico a los frutos secos, ¿este plato lleva alguno?
english: I'm allergic to tree nuts. Does this dish contain any?
tip: 'Llevar' can mean 'to contain' for food: '¿lleva alguno?' = does it contain any? 'Ser alérgico a' = to be allergic to.

target: Nos falta tiempo para todo.
english: We lack time for everything.
tip: Faltar flips English: tiempo is the subject – time is-missing on us. In Spanish you don't lack things; things go missing on you. Hence nos, not nosotros as subject.

target: Me da miedo manejar de noche.
english: I'm scared of driving at night.
tip: Fear isn't something you ARE in Spanish – things GIVE it to you: 'me da miedo' = it gives me fear. Same pattern: me da vergüenza (embarrassment), me da pena.

target: La familia es lo más importante.
english: Family is the most important thing.
tip: Why 'lo más importante,' not 'el'? With no noun to point at, Spanish uses neuter 'lo' for 'the ___ thing.' 'El más importante' would mean one specific person or item.

target: Hay una nueva política de teletrabajo.
english: There is a new remote work policy.
tip: 'Política' does double duty: policy AND politics. A 'política de teletrabajo' is a company policy; 'la política' on the news is politics. Context decides which.

target: Los lunes siempre me cuesta levantarme.
english: On Mondays it's always hard for me to get up.
tip: Cuesta here isn't about money – me cuesta levantarme means getting up costs me effort. Costar covers both prices and difficulty.

target: Mi hermano es más alto que yo.
english: My brother is taller than me.
tip: Taller than ME? Spanish says 'que yo' – comparisons take subject pronouns (yo, tú, él), never mí/ti. 'Más alto que mí' is the classic English-speaker slip.

target: No puedo respirar bien por la nariz.
english: I can't breathe well through my nose.
tip: 'Por LA nariz,' not 'mi nariz' – with body parts Spanish skips the possessive, since whose nose is obvious. Using 'mi' with your own body sounds oddly clinical.
